blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: The male and female reproductive systems are specialized to produce gametes (sperm and ova, respectively) and support fertilization and development of offspring. Understanding the anatomy and function of each organ is crucial for comprehending human reproduction.

blocks.title: Male Accessory Reproductive Organs
blocks.text:
Penis :-

  • The penis is the male external genitalia and an erectile copulatory/intromittent organ (Organ of copulation), made up of special tissue (Erectile tissue).

blocks.title: Description of Male Reproductive System
blocks.text: Description

blocks.title: Seminiferous Tubules of Male Reproductive system
blocks.text:
• The outer surface of seminiferous tubules is composed of white fibrous connective tissues called tunica propria, while the inner surface is of cuboidal germinal epithelium. This epithelium is made up of spermatogenic cells that form sperm through spermatogenesis.
  • Some columnar cells are found between the layers of the germinal epithelium and are called Sertoli cells (these occur in mammals).
  • Secretion of Cowper's gland/ Bulbourethral gland destroys acidity of the urethra and helps in lubrication of the penis.

blocks.title: Pathway of Sperms
blocks.text:
Seminiferous tubules → Straight tubule → Rete testis → Vasa efferentia → Epididymis → Vas deferens → Ampulla → Ejaculatory duct → Urethra (Prostatic urethra → Membranous urethra → Penile urethra) → Out (through urethral meatus).

  • Semen = Sperm + Accessory reproductive gland fluid
  • Volume = 3-4 ml.
  • Normal sperm count = 20 to 120 million/ml.
  • A human male ejaculates about 200 to 300 million sperm per coitus.
  • For normal fertility, at least 60 percent must have normal shape and size of sperm and at least 40 percent of them must show vigorous motility.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
How many testicular lobules are present in each testis ?

(1) About 100

(2) About 150

(3) About 250

(4) Infinite
blocks.answer:
Ans- 3

Testicular lobules are compartments within the testis that contain one to four highly coiled seminiferous tubules. The testis is an oval structure that is about 5 cm long and 3 cm in diameter. A tough, white fibrous connective tissue capsule called the tunica albuginea surrounds the testis and extends inward to form septa that partition the organ into lobules.
blocks.prompt: How many testicular lobules are present in each testis ?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Correct order of spermatogenesis is :-

(1) Spermatocytes, Spermatogonium, Spermatids, Sperms

(2) Spermatogonium, Spermatids, Spermatocytes, Sperms

(3) Spermatids, Spermatogonium, Spermatocytes, Sperms

(4) Spermatogonium, Primary Spermatocytes, Secondary Spermatocytes, Spermatids, Sperms
blocks.answer:
Ans-4

The correct order of spermatogenesis is spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and spermatozoa:

  • Spermatogonia: The starting point of spermatogenesis
  • Primary spermatocytes: Spermatogonia that grow in size and gather nourishing substances
  • Secondary spermatocytes: Formed after meiosis I, these cells are haploid, meaning they contain half the number of chromosomes
  • Spermatids: Immature sperm that undergo cell differentiation to become mature spermatozoa
  • Spermatozoa: The final product of spermatogenesis
options: (4) Spermatogonium, Primary Spermatocytes, Secondary Spermatocytes, Spermatids, Sperms

modules.name: Female Reproductive System, Gametogenesis and Menstrual Cycle

blocks.title: Female Reproductive System
blocks.text:
Located in the pelvic region

  • It consists of a pair of ovaries along with a pair of oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina, and external genitalia located in pelvis.
  • Mammary glands, Fallopian tube, Uterus, and Vagina = Secondary sex organs
  • Vagina = Female Copulatory Organ = Fibromuscular + Non-glandular tube like organ
  • Birth Canal = Cervical canal + Vagina
  • Vulva includes = Mons veneris, Labia Majora, Labia Minora, Clitoris(Homologus to penis in males), Hymen, Vestibules and related perineum.

blocks.title: Gametogenesis
blocks.text:
Spermatogenesis :-

Spermiogenesis and spermiation : Transformation of spermatids into sperms is spermiogenesis.  After spermiogenesis, sperm heads become embedded in the Sertoli cells and are finally released from seminiferous tubules by a process called spermiation.

blocks.title: Previous Year Question 1
blocks.question:
During spermatogenesis, how many spermatozoa are formed from a single primary spermatocyte ?

(1) 1

(2) 2

(3) 4

(4) 8
blocks.answer:
Ans- 3

  • During spermatogenesis, a single primary spermatocyte (which is diploid, 2n) undergoes meiosis to form spermatozoa.
  • The primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic division (Meiosis I) to produce two secondary spermatocytes (haploid, n).
  • Each secondary spermatocyte undergoes the second meiotic division (Meiosis II) to form two spermatids.
  • Each of these four spermatids matures into a functional spermatozoon (plural: spermatozoa) during the process of spermiogenesis.
blocks.prompt: During spermatogenesis, how many spermatozoa are formed from a single primary spermatocyte ?

blocks.title: Structure of Sperm
blocks.text:
The structure of sperm consists of three main parts:

  • Head: Contains the nucleus, which holds the genetic material (DNA), and the acrosome, a cap that helps penetrate the egg. The acrosome contains sperm lysins, which help in fertilization.
  • Middle piece: Packed with mitochondria that provide the energy necessary for sperm motility ( Nebenkern Sheath).
  • Tail: A long, whip-like structure that propels the sperm forward, allowing it to swim towards the egg.

blocks.title: Oogenesis
blocks.text:
Oogenesis :-    • It is the process of egg (ovum) production.
    • It occurs in the ovaries and involves the development and maturation of female gametes (ova) from primordial germ cells.
    • During embryonic development couple of million gamete mother cells (oogonia) are formed in each fetal ovary.
    • No more oogonia are formed/added after birth in females.

blocks.title: Menstrual Cycle
blocks.text:
Menstrual Cycle :-

Phases of the Menstrual Cycle :-

  • Menstrual Phase (Days 1-5): Shedding of uterine lining.
  • Follicular Phase (Days 1-13): FSH stimulates follicle growth; estrogen rises.
  • Ovulation (Day 14): LH surge triggers ovum release.
  • Luteal Phase (Days 15-28): Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, maintaining uterine lining.

blocks.title: Points To Remember
blocks.text:
Key Hormones

  • FSH: Stimulates follicle growth.
  • LH: Triggers ovulation.
  • Estrogen: Builds endometrial lining.
  • Progesterone: Maintains endometrial lining.
Important Structures

  • Graafian Follicle: Mature ovarian follicle.
  • Corpus Luteum: Post-ovulation structure from ruptured follicle.
Equations and Facts

  • Chromosome Number:
  • Spermatogenesis: $2n \rightarrow n$
  • Oogenesis: $2n \rightarrow n$
  • Cycle Duration: Average menstrual cycle is 28 days.
Strategic Approaches

  • Use mnemonic: "Menstruation, Follicular, Ovulation, Luteal (MFOL)" for cycle phases.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Fertilization: Fusion of male and female gametes (sperm and ovum) forming a diploid zygote.
  • Implantation: Attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine wall, initiating pregnancy.

blocks.title: Fertilisation and Implantation
blocks.text:
• Fertilization Site: Occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube.
  • Sperm Capacitation: Enables sperm to penetrate the ovum; occurs in the female reproductive tract.
  • Acrosome Reaction: Enzymes released from sperm's acrosome penetrate the ovum's zona pellucida.
  • Cortical Reaction: Modifies the zona pellucida to prevent polyspermy after the first sperm enters.
  • Formation of Zygote: Fusion of sperm and ovum nuclei creates a diploid zygote, which undergoes mitotic divisions to form a morula and then a blastocyst.
  • Trophoblast: Aids implantation and placenta formation.
  • Inner Cell Mass (ICM): Develops into the embryo.
  • Apposition: Initial contact with the endometrium.
  • Adhesion: Tight binding to the uterine wall.
  • Invasion: Trophoblast cells invade the endometrium.
  • hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin): Secreted by the trophoblast, maintains corpus luteum and progesterone production.

↓

↓

Formation of Male Pronucleus
↓

Migration of Male and Female Pronuclei
↓

Karyogamy and Amphimixis

  • Syngamy = Union of male and female gametes is called syngamy.
  • Karyogamy = Fusion of pronuclei of sperm and ovum.
  • Amphimixis = Intermingling of their Chromosomes.

blocks.title: Sex Determination
blocks.text:
• The male gametes (sperms) the sex chromosome could be either X or Y, hence, 50 per cent of sperms carry the X chromosome while the other 50 per cent carry the Y.
  • After fusion of the male and female gametes the zygote would carry either XX or XY depending on whether the sperm carrying X or Y fertilized the ovum.
  • The zygote carrying XX would develop into a female baby and XY would form a male.

blocks.title: Previous Year Question 3
blocks.question:
Placenta in human beings is formed by :-

(1) amnion

(2) chorion

(3) allantois

(4) chorion and uterine wall
blocks.answer:
Ans- 4

The placenta in humans is formed by the chorion and the uterine wall:

  • Chorion: The fetal part of the placenta
  • Uterine wall: The maternal part of the placenta

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: Pregnancy begins with the implantation of the blastocyst into the uterine wall and continues with embryonic and fetal development up to birth. Key processes include cell division, differentiation, and organogenesis, regulated by hormonal changes.

blocks.title: Hormones of Placenta
blocks.text: Hormones of Placenta

blocks.title: Embryonic Development
blocks.text:
Embryonic development, as outlined in NCERT content, covers the stages of development from fertilization to the formation of a mature organism. Key stages include:

  • Fertilization: The sperm and egg unite to form a zygote.
  • Cleavage: The zygote undergoes rapid cell division, leading to a multicellular structure called the morula.
  • Blastulation: The morula develops into a blastocyst, featuring an inner cell mass that will form the embryo and an outer layer that will contribute to the placenta.
  • Gastrulation: The blastocyst undergoes significant reorganization, forming three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, which will differentiate into various tissues and organs.
  • Organogenesis: The germ layers develop into specific organs and systems, marking the transition to a recognizable embryo.
  • Embryo: Early stages of pregnancy from the time of fertilization up to 8 weeks.
  • Fetus: Develops pregnancy from the end of 8 weeks till birth of the baby.

blocks.title: Parturition
blocks.text:
Process of delivery of the fetus (childbirth)

Complex neuroendocrine mechanism.

• Soon after the infant is delivered, the placenta is also expelled out of the uterus.

blocks.title: Previous Year Question 1
blocks.question:
In gastrula stage, which layer(s) is/are formed ?

(1) ectoderm (2) mesoderm

(3) endoderm (4) All of the above
blocks.answer:
ANSWER = 4

All of the germ layers, ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, are formed during the gastrula stage:

blocks.title: Lactation
blocks.text:
• The mammary glands of the female undergo differentiation during pregnancy and start producing milk towards the end of pregnancy by the process called lactation.

• The milk produced during the initial few days of lactation is called colostrum which contains several antibodies essential to develop resistance for newborn babies.

Fetus: Human from end of 8th week to birth
Prolactin: Milk production and rich in antibodies.
Colostrum: First milk, rich in antibodies
Lactation Reflex: Stimulates prolactin and oxytocin
Remember oxytocin's dual role in labor/lactation

blocks.title: Previous Year Question 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following is not true about the parturition process?

(1) Secretion of oxytocin hormone by posterior pituitary

(2) Narrowing of pelvic cavity by relaxin hormone

(3) Secretion of progesterone hormone is stopped

(4) General position of fetus is occipital-anterior
blocks.answer:
Ans- 2

The statement that is not true about the parturition process is that the pelvic cavity does not narrow due to the relaxin hormone.

In an occipital-anterior position, the body's head is down, and the back of the head (occiput) is facing the mother's front (anterior side), a normal and ideal birth position.
options: (1) Secretion of oxytocin hormone by posterior pituitary
(2) Narrowing of pelvic cavity by relaxin hormone
(3) Secretion of progesterone hormone is stopped
(4) General position of fetus is occipital-anterior
